podcast.title: 70s Decline and Resurgence
podcast.body: By the end of the 1970s, Bubblegum Music ceded its prominence, passing the torch to punk and giving way on the Billboard charts to disco. However, it experienced a significant resurgence in the late 1990s and continued into the early 21st century, with artists like Britney Spears, the Spice Girls, and NSYNC. "By the end of the 70s, Bubblegum Music had passed the torch on to punk and it gave way on the Billboard charts to disco It would rise again in the late 90s and into the early 21st century with the likes of Britney Spears and the Spice Girls and NSYNC and the like."

Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Critical Reception
podcast.body: Bubblegum music faced significant resistance from rock critics who often published scathing reviews, primarily due to concerns about a lack of "authenticity," especially when record labels intentionally targeted preteens. They were also bothered by "fake bands" scoring mega hits. "The fact though that an artist or a record label would intentionally seek the dollar of preteens who are presumed to have bad taste in music is exactly what turned off the vast majority of rock critics."

Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Definition and Target Audience
podcast.body: Bubblegum music refers both to its sound, typically uptempo dance music with uncomplicated lyrics, and the age group it is marketed to, generally 12 to 16-year-olds, with slight variations. "The term refers as much to the age group that the music is marketed to as it does to the sound which is generally uptempo dance music with uncomplicated lyrics. The age group for marketing was roughly 12 to 16."

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music
Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Demand for Teen Idols
podcast.body: Ron Tepper, a marketer for a Los Angeles company, observed that demand for teen idols could not be manufactured; they either fit what teenagers wanted or they didn't. If they fit, merchandise and records sold; if not, "you could not give those records away." "Ron Tepper was a marketer for the law for a company in Los Angeles and he said that you could not generate demand for teen idols. They either fit the mold of what the teenagers wanted or they did not."

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music
Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Enduring Memorability
podcast.body: Many Bubblegum Music songs have demonstrated remarkable staying power, remaining memorable and enduring for decades after their initial release. This longevity is often attributed to the quality of their composition and musicianship. "There is a reason why many of these songs endure and are memorable decades later."

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music
Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Evolution into Teen Idol Market
podcast.body: In the early 1970s in the United States, bubblegum music morphed into a phenomenon closely associated with teen idols, who also sold merchandise like *Tiger Beat* and *16 Magazine* posters and lunchboxes. While teen idols were "real" people unlike cartoon bands, from a musical standpoint, there was little to differentiate them from bubblegum acts. "So in the early 70s we start to see at least in the United States bubble gum morphs into the succession with teen idols who will also sell Tiger Beat or 16 magazine posters, lunch boxes."

Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: High-Caliber Contributors
podcast.body: The genre benefited from the involvement of some of Pop's best writers, such as Neil Diamond, who penned songs for Bubblegum artists. Additionally, top-tier session musicians, including Joe Walsh, played on many Bubblegum tracks, for example, with the Ohio Express. "Some of Pop's best writers wrote songs for Bubblegum, Neil Diamond comes to mind And some of the best session musicians played on these songs, Joe Walsh played on some of the Ohio Express songs."

srcs.episode: Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music
Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Historical Counterpoint to Serious Rock
podcast.body: Bubblegum music is described as the conceptual opposite of the "hard and serious rock" prevalent in the 1960s and early 1970s. This comparison highlights Tweetpop's similar role as a gentle alternative within the alt-rock landscape, but with the crucial distinction of avoiding the negative connotations often associated with bubblegum music. "If Bubblegum music was the opposite of hard and serious rock of the 1960s and early 1970s, Tweetpop is that to the alt rock world."

podcast.title: Industry Perspective on Quality
podcast.body: Steve Wax, a public relations representative for Bell Records in the early 1970s, emphasized that "good and bad are relative terms" in bubblegum music, arguing that if people want a particular "product," it should be provided, regardless of personal taste. "Steve Wax who was a public relations representative for Bell Records in the early 70s said, bubblegum music you've got to remember that good and bad are relative terms people say to me how can you promote that stuff but I'm paid to do a job so what do my personal likes have to do with it if that's what the people want how can I deny it to them."

podcast.title: Irony of Authenticity (Lester Bangs)
podcast.body: Lester Bangs highlighted the "wonderful irony" that despite many bubblegum groups never truly existing, there was an "authentic tenderness" in their performance of sentimental lyrics. "The wonderful irony is that it worked and even if most of these groups never really existed. There was an authentic tenderness they meant when they sang, oh sugar sugar honey you are my candy girl I can't stop wanting you."

podcast.title: Lester Bangs' Definition
podcast.body: Rock critic Lester Bangs famously described bubblegum music as "the basic sound of rock and roll minus the rage, fear, violence and enemy that runs from Johnny Burnett to Sid Vicious." "the basic sound of rock and roll minus the rage, fear, violence and enemy that runs from Johnny Burnett to Sid Vicious."

Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Marketing as "Product"
podcast.body: Trade magazines like *Billboard* frequently used the term "product" when referring to the music of both cartoon bubblegum bands and real teen idols, emphasizing the heavy marketing aspect of this genre. "If you read some of these old trade magazines like Billboard, you will note that the word product is used when referring to the music of both the cartoon bands and the real teen idols because it's a lot about marketing."

Ep. 30 - The Sweet Sound of 70s Bubblegum Music

podcast.title: Non-Political Content
podcast.body: Bubblegum Music, as a genre, typically did not engage with social issues or politics in its lyrical content. Despite this, its quality was often high due to the caliber of its contributors. "While this music did not comment on social issues or politics."

podcast.title: Simon Frith's Perspective on Pop
podcast.body: Simon Frith, a former professor of music studies and rock critic, stated that pop music is "for public use" and its purpose is partly to make a profit by giving people what they already want, rather than pushing boundaries. This formulaic approach doesn't necessarily make it "bad." "Simon Frith... has stated that pop music is for public use. That means in part that the purpose of pop music is to make a profit."

podcast.title: Teen Idol Sexuality and Marketing
podcast.body: Fred Rice, a promoter for The Jacksons, commented that the bubblegum audience required teen idols who were "not a sexual threat," suggesting that having a picture of David Cassidy or Donnie Osmond on a pillow was analogous to "sleeping with them" in a non-threatening way. "Fred Rice who was a promoter for the Jackson's said that the bubblegum audience needed teen idols that were not a sexual threat. To have a picture of David Cassidy or Donnie Osmond on their pillow was like sleeping with them."
